query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor interstitial addition of boron into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will improve its load‐bearing integrity by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and retarding crack initiation while leaving the underlying order–disorder transition (mediated by chemical short-range order) essentially unchanged.
generation.material_initial_state: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy, which exhibits large caloric responses under applied fields and pressure but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor interstitial addition of boron during alloy preparation.
generation.conditions: Test under similar operative applied magnetic/pressure fields and near‐room temperature conditions as the original alloy; the boron addition level is kept low enough to avoid shifting the phase-transition boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries in the polycrystalline alloy, where boron is expected to segregate and increase cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially segregate to grain boundaries, reducing stress concentrations and retarding crack initiation/propagation. Since the caloric effect originates from an order–disorder transition (mediated by chemical short-range order) within the alloy’s lattice, the minor boron addition does not significantly disturb this transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in fracture toughness and load‐bearing capacity (with reduced crack propagation) while the magnitude of the caloric performance (e.g., entropy change under applied fields/pressures) remains essentially unchanged relative to the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated alloy shows a strong caloric response but exhibits cracking and poor load‐bearing integrity under operating conditions.
generation.boundary: Operative fields, pressures, and temperatures remain within the existing operating regime; the boron addition is minimal to ensure that phase stability and caloric transition temperatures remain unaltered.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of low-level boron doping on both the mechanical integrity and any subtle effects on the caloric transition is not precisely determined and needs experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and a second set doped with 0.1–0.5 at% boron. Measure mechanical properties (e.g., fracture toughness, crack propagation under standardized loading tests) and caloric performance (e.g., entropy and temperature change under applied pressure/field cycles) under identical conditions.
measurements: Fracture toughness and stress–strain response under mechanical loading
Caloric effect metrics (e.g., entropy change, adiabatic temperature change) under controlled applied-field and pressure-field cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in load-bearing integrity (e.g., higher fracture toughness or reduced cracking) without a concomitant reduction (beyond experimental variation) in the caloric response compared to the undoped alloy, or if the doping adversely alters the phase-transition characteristics, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
